title: "First Steps"

## The development loop

Before touching any feature code, internalize this cycle. Every working session repeats it:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    E["✏️ Edit<br>VS Code"] --> B["🔨 Build<br>cmake --build build"]
    B --> R["▶️ Run<br>./freud.exe ..."]
    R --> C["📦 Commit<br>git commit -m '...'"]
    C --> P["🚀 Push<br>git push"]
    P --> PL["⬇️ Teammates pull<br>git pull"]
    PL --> E
```

The first time (or after changing `CMakeLists.txt`), also run configure and install:

```bash
cmake -B build           # configure — run once, or after CMakeLists changes
cmake --build build      # compile
cmake --install build    # install
./freud.exe --debug -f images/input/image.jpeg -c helloworld
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Always end a session with a push.** GitHub Actions evaluate what is on `main`. Code that stays on your machine is invisible to your teammates and the evaluator.
:::

## Milestone 1 — Learn together (mob programming) {#milestone-1}

Milestone 1 is the **Tutorial** milestone. Its five issues are not distributed one per person — they are solved together, rotating who types at the keyboard.

### Why mob programming for Milestone 1?

The goal is that **everyone** on the team understands:

- How the project compiles and runs
- How image data is structured in memory
- The exact pattern to add a new feature (header → implementation → manifest)
- How to commit and push

If one person solves all five issues alone, the others miss the learning. This will hurt everyone in the **individual, closed-book final exam** where no one can ask a teammate for help.

### The rotation rhythm

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant S1 as Student 1 (keyboard)
    participant S2 as Student 2 (watching)
    participant S3 as Student 3 (watching)
    participant GH as GitHub

    Note over S1,S3: Everyone gathers at Student 1's screen
    Note over S1,S3: Read Issue #3 together — discuss the solution
    S1->>S1: Implement, build, run
    S1->>GH: git commit + push

    Note over S1,S3: Move to Student 2's screen
    S2->>GH: git pull
    Note over S1,S3: Read Issue #4 together — discuss the solution
    S2->>S2: Implement, build, run
    S2->>GH: git commit + push

    Note over S1,S3: Move to Student 3's screen
    S3->>GH: git pull
    Note over S1,S3: Read Issue #5 together — discuss the solution
    S3->>S3: Implement, build, run
    S3->>GH: git commit + push

    Note over S1,S3: Continue rotating for Issues #6 and #7
```

**Rules:**

- Everyone watches, everyone talks. The person at the keyboard types.
- Each student must commit and push at least once during Milestone 1.
- Do **not** split the five issues and work in parallel — that defeats the entire purpose of Milestone 1.

### Milestone 1 issues (Tutorial)

| # | Feature | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|
| [#3](../Features/issues/feature-3-dimension.md) | Dimension | Open an image, read width and height |
| [#4](../Features/issues/feature-4-color-of-the-first-pixel.md) | Color of the first pixel | Access pixel data, index into the array |
| [#5](../Features/issues/feature-5-color-of-the-10th-pixel.md) | Color of the 10th pixel | Offset arithmetic in a pixel array |
| [#6](../Features/issues/feature-6-color-of-the-first-pixel-on-the-second-line.md) | First pixel, second line | 2D indexing: row × width + column |
| [#7](../Features/issues/feature-7-rgb-pixel-get-and-print-functions.md) | RGB pixel get and print | Reusable helper functions |

## Later milestones — Collaborative workflow {#later-milestones}

Once everyone understands the basics from Milestone 1, you can distribute effort across features. **Distributing work does not mean working in isolation.**

### Recommended per-feature workflow

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["🤝 Team gathers<br>Choose next feature<br>Read the issue spec together"] --> B["✍️ One member writes:<br>• function signature in features.h<br>• stub call in main.c<br>(compiles but does nothing yet)"]
    B --> C["git commit + push"]
    C --> D["Everyone: git pull"]
    D --> E["💻 Implement the feature body<br>in features.c"]
    E --> F["Build · Run · Check output<br>against issue spec"]
    F --> G["git commit + push"]
    G --> H["Next feature →"]
```

**Why gather first?** Agreeing on the function signature before anyone codes prevents most merge conflicts and ensures the feature matches the spec.

### Roles (rotate each session)

| Role | What they do |
|---|---|
| **Integrator** | Merges branches, resolves conflicts, monitors CI results |
| **Coder** | Implements a specific feature |
| **Reviewer** | Tests locally, checks output format against the issue spec |

::: {.callout-warning}
**Rotate roles every session.** The final exam is individual and without any resources. Every student must have coded features, managed git, and debugged builds on their own at least once before the exam.
:::

## Where to code {#where-to-code}

All feature code lives in three files:

| File | What to do there |
|---|---|
| `src/features.h` | Declare function prototypes |
| `src/features.c` | Implement functions |
| `freud.manifest` | Add the command name (one per line) |

`main.c` routes the `-c` command to features. Copy this pattern for each new feature:

```c
if ( strncmp( configuration.command, "helloworld", 10 ) == 0 ) {
    /* helloWorld() is declared in features.h, implemented in features.c */
    helloWorld();
}
```

Example `freud.manifest` after adding `dimension`:

```text
helloworld
dimension
```

## Configuration structure

The command-line parser fills a `Config` structure available as `configuration` in `main.c`:

```c
#define MAX_FILE_COUNT 10
#define MAX_LENGTH_COMMAND 25
#define MAX_ARGUMENT_COUNT 5

typedef struct _config {
    int debug_mode;
    char command[MAX_LENGTH_COMMAND];
    char* filenames[MAX_FILE_COUNT];
    char* arguments[MAX_ARGUMENT_COUNT];
} Config;
```

Fields you will use most:

- `configuration.command` — value passed to `-c`
- `configuration.filenames[0]` — image path passed to `-f`
- `configuration.arguments[0]` — first extra argument (used by some features, e.g., `R`, `G`, or `B`)

## VS Code run configuration

To avoid retyping the command every time, update `cmake.debugConfig.args` in `.vscode/settings.json` with your target image path and command. The VS Code Run button will then use those arguments directly.
